name: Kaş
desc: A shelf of white houses and bougainvillea stacked above a harbour that looks straight at the Greek island of Meis. A Hellenistic theatre sits five minutes from the square, a Lycian sarcophagus stands in the middle of a shopping street, and the evenings are meze, grilled fish and jasmine.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — August is hot and the town doubles in size
tip: Hand your passport to the ferry office by the harbour the evening before you sail to Meis, not on the morning itself.
rev: Visitors love the scale, the food and the diving; the recurring gripes are the parking, the steep haul back up from the harbour, and the fact that the town itself has no real beach.
entry: Free — the theatre and the Lion Tomb are open street-side
onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM) airport, then the D400 coast road — roughly 3.5 h from either, Dalaman usually the easier drive.

name: Kalkan
desc: An old Greek-built harbour village of steep whitewashed lanes that has quietly turned into a hillside of villas with private pools. The draw is the rooftop restaurants above the bay and the light at dusk on Kalkan's amphitheatre of houses; the flaw is the near-total absence of sand.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the hill streets are an oven at noon in August
tip: Swim from one of the beach-club platforms below the old town rather than hunting for a beach that does not exist.
todo: Sunset drink on an old-town roof terrace
Boat to Kaputaş and the blue caves
Walk the harbour breakwater after dark
rev: Repeat visitors rate the villa comfort and the restaurant standard highly, while first-timers complain about the vertical streets, taxi prices and how British the high season feels.
entry: Free
onward: Dalaman (DLM) airport, then about 2 h on the D400; Antalya (AYT) is 3.5–4 h east.

name: Kaputaş Beach
desc: A wedge of pale gravel at the mouth of a gorge, reached by 180-odd steps down from the Kaş–Kalkan road. The water is an improbable turquoise because cold karst springs surface here, which also makes it noticeably colder than the open sea. Small, photogenic and completely exposed.
season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for photographs without the crowd
tip: Come before 10:00 or after 17:00 — midday the stairs, the two sunbed rows and the roadside parking are all full at once.
todo: Photograph the bay from the road bridge
Kayak into the Blue Cave nearby
rev: Everyone agrees the colour is real; the complaints are the stair climb in heat, the shadeless afternoon, the cold undertow and periodic closures after rockfall on the cliff above.
entry: Free — sunbeds around ₺400 (≈€9) a pair
onward: Dalaman (DLM) or Antalya (AYT), then the D400 — the beach is 7 km east of Kalkan with a lay-by on both sides of the road.

name: Patara
desc: Lycia's old capital and harbour, half-buried in dunes behind an 12-kilometre beach. The re-erected bouleuterion where the Lycian League voted, a triple-arched gate standing alone in a field, and the oldest known lighthouse in the world, rebuilt block by block from its fallen pieces.
season: Apr–May and Oct — midsummer is shadeless and the sand radiates heat
tip: One ticket covers the ruins and the beach behind them, so do the site first and walk out to the sand rather than driving back.
todo: Sit in the restored Lycian League parliament
Walk the colonnaded street to the granary
See the rebuilt lighthouse by the shore
rev: Praised as the rare ancient city with a beach attached; visitors grumble about the heat, the mosquitoes from the marsh at dusk and how little shade or signage there is between monuments.
entry: €15 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Dalaman (DLM) 1.5 h or Antalya (AYT) 3.5 h, then 4 km down the lane from the D400 through Gelemiş village.

name: Xanthos
desc: The Lycian capital on a bluff above the Eşen river, twice destroyed by its own citizens rather than surrender. Pillar tombs stand at odd angles beside a Roman theatre, and the Harpy Tomb reliefs on site are casts — Charles Fellows shipped the originals to the British Museum in 1842.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — flowering slopes in spring, brutal glare in July
tip: Walk up past the theatre to the acropolis for the view over the whole Xanthos valley; almost every coach group turns back at the pillar tombs.
todo: Harpy Tomb and the pillar sarcophagus
rev: Archaeology-minded visitors call it the most important Lycian site in Türkiye; others find it bare and are annoyed that the best sculpture is in London and the labelling is thin.
entry: €3 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Dalaman (DLM) about 1 h 15, then the D400 to Kınık village; the site is signposted on the main road.

name: Kaş Diving
desc: The clearest, best-organised diving in Türkiye: twenty-odd sites within twenty minutes of the harbour, thirty-metre visibility and walls that drop straight off the Uluburun cape. There is a sunken passenger plane at eighteen metres, amphora fields, and the reef where the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck was found in 1982.
season: May–Nov — water is 16 °C in March, 27 °C in late August
tip: Book two-tank morning boats: the afternoon wind gets up off Uluburun and the visibility drops with the swell.
todo: Uluburun wall and the wreck site
rev: Divers rate the schools and the marine-park rules highly; complaints centre on how bare the reefs are of big fish after decades of fishing, and on peak-season boats stacked at the same buoy.
entry: Two-tank day around €70–90 with kit; try-dives from about €55
onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM), then the D400 to Kaş; all the dive schools are on the harbour front, no car needed.

name: Kekova
desc: A long uninhabited island whose northern shore slid into the sea in a second-century earthquake. From a boat you look down on staircases, doorways and cut foundations a metre under clear water, with the odd sarcophagus lid breaking the surface offshore.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — flat mornings, and the day boats thin out after September
tip: Swimming and diving over the sunken city are banned; take a kayak or a small gulet from Üçağız at 09:00 instead of the big Kaş boats that arrive at noon.
todo: Glass-bottom pass over the sunken stairs
rev: Reliably called the best boat day on the Lycian coast, though people are surprised how little is actually visible from a hull, and midday convoys of tour boats spoil the quiet.
entry: Free to look; boat from Üçağız around ₺1,200–1,800 (≈€26–40) for a shared day
onward: Antalya (AYT) 2.5 h or Dalaman (DLM) 3 h, then the lane south from the D400 at Çevreli down to Üçağız harbour.

name: Simena (Kaleköy)
desc: A car-free village of thirty houses climbing to a crusader castle, reached only by boat or on foot. Inside the walls is the smallest ancient theatre in Lycia, cut for about three hundred people, and the view takes in the whole Kekova channel and a sarcophagus standing in the water below.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — most pensions shut from November to March
tip: Stay the night: after the last day boat leaves at five the village belongs to about a dozen guests and the goats.
rev: Almost everyone calls the castle view the best on this coast; the complaints are the steep stepped path with luggage, the castle ticket booth and inflated prices at the waterside restaurants.
entry: Castle ₺200 (≈€4.50) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM), then drive to Üçağız and take a 10-minute water taxi; there is no road into the village.

name: Üçağız (Teimiussa)
desc: A fishing hamlet on a sheltered lagoon where the Lycian necropolis runs right down to the waterline — rock-cut tombs standing among the boats, some with their lids half in the sea. It is the launching point for Kekova and, for two hours after the boats leave, one of the quietest places on the coast.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — dead quiet and half-shut in winter
tip: Walk east ten minutes past the last house to the necropolis at Teimiussa, where nobody goes and the tombs sit in open scrub.
rev: Praised as an easy, unpolished base with good pensions; the standard grumbles are aggressive boat touts on the quay, weak mobile signal and the long unlit road in.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) 2.5 h, then 19 km of narrow lane south from the D400 at Çevreli; dolmuşes run from Demre in summer only.

name: Myra
desc: A cliff face honeycombed with house-shaped Lycian tombs above a Roman theatre whose stage blocks are carved with theatrical masks. Recent digs under the greenhouses have uncovered a second, older theatre and painted terracotta figures, so the site keeps growing while you visit.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the greenhouse plain traps heat in summer
tip: Go first thing: the tombs face south-west, so morning light flattens them and the afternoon is when the cruise buses from Demre arrive.
todo: Rock tombs from the theatre steps
Carved masks on the stage wall
rev: The tomb façade impresses everyone; complaints are that the site is small for the price, the fence keeps you well back from the cliff, and tour groups fill the theatre in bursts.
entry: €13 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h on the D400 to Demre, then 2 km up through the tomato greenhouses.

name: Church of St. Nicholas, Demre
desc: The Byzantine church built over the grave of the fourth-century bishop who became Father Christmas, sunk several metres below today's street level. Inside are opus sectile floors, faded frescoes of saints and the broken sarcophagus Italian sailors raided in 1087, all under a protective steel roof.
season: All year — spring and autumn avoid both heat and the Orthodox pilgrimage peaks
tip: Come before 10:00 or after 16:00; Russian and Ukrainian pilgrim coaches fill the nave in the middle of the day and photography becomes hopeless.
todo: Mosaic floor of the south aisle
rev: Historically extraordinary, say most; the repeated criticisms are the high foreigner ticket, the scaffolding-like shelter overhead and the tat market you walk through to reach the door.
entry: €17 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h by car or the Kaş-bound bus to Demre; the church is in the town centre, five minutes from the otogar.

name: Andriake
desc: Myra's port, where St Paul changed ships on the way to Rome. Hadrian's granary still stands almost to roof height with the emperor's portrait bust over the door, and it now houses the Museum of Lycian Civilisations. Beyond it a reed marsh full of herons runs out to Çayağzı beach.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the marsh breeds mosquitoes in high summer
tip: The site ticket includes the museum in the granary, and the boardwalk over the marsh to the sea is the part almost nobody walks.
rev: Visitors find it refreshingly empty next to Myra and rate the museum well; the drawbacks are almost no shade, sparse English labels and a car park that floods after winter rain.
entry: €6 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Demre, then 5 km down to the harbour road at Çayağzı, where the Kekova boats also leave.

name: Arycanda
desc: Lycia's best-sited city, built on five terraces against a mountain wall above the Finike–Elmalı road. The bath house still has arched windows framing the valley, the stadium sits on a shelf above the theatre, and you often have the whole slope to yourself with only cowbells for noise.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow can reach the upper terraces in winter
tip: Climb to the stadium at the very top before you look at anything else; the drop back down through the theatre is the whole point of the place.
rev: Repeatedly described as the most beautiful ruin in Lycia and almost deserted; the caveats are the steep uneven climb, no café or shade, and a warden who sometimes shuts early out of season.
entry: ₺180 (≈€4) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h — take the D635 inland from Finike toward Elmalı; the site is signed on the left after 30 km.

name: Olympos
desc: A pirate city swallowed by jungle: bay leaves, figs and oleander growing through a temple gate, a Roman bridge abutment and Byzantine walls along a stream bed that runs down to a pebble beach. You walk the whole site inside a green tunnel, which is why it stays bearable in summer.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the creek dries and the mosquitoes arrive in August
tip: The beach is only reachable through the ruins on the same ticket, and the gate closes at sunset — swim early, not after dinner.
todo: Carved temple doorway by the stream
Necropolis path on the north bank
rev: The treehouse-village atmosphere and the overgrown ruins win people over; the complaints are the ticketed beach access, the mosquitoes, and how loud the valley's backpacker bars get in July.
entry: €10 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 20 on the D400, then 11 km down a steep switchback lane from the Olympos junction.

name: Çıralı
desc: Three kilometres of pebble backed by orange groves and small family pensions, with building height capped because loggerhead turtles nest on the sand. No hotel blocks, no jet skis, a stream mouth cold enough to make you gasp, and the Chimaera flames burning on the ridge behind.
season: May–Oct for swimming; Apr and Nov for walking, with pensions open most of the year
tip: Between May and October the beach is roped and closed after dark for the nesting turtles — respect it, and never light a fire or a torch on the sand.
todo: Walk the beach to the Olympos ruins
rev: People come back yearly for the quiet and the pensions; the honest downsides are the sharp pebbles, the winding access road, limited food choice and shops that close early out of season.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 15 on the D400, then 7 km down the Ulupınar valley road; buses drop you at the junction and a minibus meets them.

name: Yanartaş (Chimaera)
desc: Two dozen flames burning straight out of bare rock on a hillside above Çıralı, fed by methane seeping from the serpentinite and alight for at least two and a half thousand years. Homer's fire-breathing Chimaera was located here, and the ruins of a Hephaestus temple sit just below the vents.
season: All year, best Oct–Apr when the nights are cold enough to make the flames vivid
tip: Go up after dark with a head torch — in daylight the flames are almost invisible and the twenty-minute stone path is the whole disappointment people report.
todo: Night walk down with the sea lights below
rev: Magical after dark, say most; the standard complaints are that the flames are smaller than the photos suggest, the rocky climb is harder than advertised, and the car park now charges too.
entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) plus parking
onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 15, then the Çıralı road; the trailhead is 3 km beyond the village, followed by a 20–30 min climb.

name: Adrasan
desc: A two-kilometre bay closed at both ends by pine ridges, with a shingle beach, a river mouth and low pensions instead of resorts. It is the calmest swimming water on this stretch and the departure point for boats to Suluada and the Ceneviz coves that you cannot reach by road.
season: Jun–Sep for the water; May and Oct for walking the Lycian Way sections above the bay
tip: Take the small local boat to Ceneviz bay rather than the big Antalya day-trip gulets — it leaves at 10:00 from the river-mouth jetty and holds a dozen people.
todo: Walk up Musa Dağı for the bay view
rev: Regulars value the low-key family feel and the sheltered water; complaints are the stony beach, the mosquitoes near the river and a village that essentially closes between November and April.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 30 on the D400, then 12 km down from the Çavuşköy turning past Kumluca.

name: Cape Gelidonya Lighthouse
desc: The southern tip of the Teke peninsula, where a small stone lighthouse looks out over the Beşadalar — five bare islets in open sea. The path in from Karaöz is one of the best hours of the Lycian Way, and the seabed off the cape gave up a Bronze Age shipwreck excavated in 1960.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade at all on the cape in summer
tip: Drive to Karaöz and walk the last 4 km; ordinary cars regularly get stuck on the rutted track beyond the last houses.
todo: Walk the coast path from Karaöz
rev: Hikers call the approach the finest stretch of the whole trail; the warnings are the exposed heat, no water source, an unmarked final section and a lighthouse you cannot go inside.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 45 to Kumluca, then the Mavikent–Karaöz road; the last stretch to the cape is on foot.

name: Suluada
desc: An uninhabited islet off Adrasan with two white sand coves and water so pale it gets called the Turkish Maldives, which for once is not far off. There is nothing on it — no shade, no kiosk, no jetty — so boats anchor offshore and you swim the last twenty metres in.
season: Jun–Sep only; the crossing is cancelled in any real wind
tip: Take the first boat out of Adrasan at 09:30 and you get an hour before the Antalya day-trip fleet turns up and moors six deep.
rev: The colour lives up to the photos; the complaints are relentless — packed boats with loud music, no facilities, no shade and rubbish left by day-trippers on a protected island.
entry: Free island; boat from Adrasan around ₺1,000–1,500 (≈€22–33) per person
onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 30 to Adrasan or Çıralı, then a 45-minute boat crossing; there is no scheduled ferry.

name: Phaselis
desc: Three natural harbours joined by a marble main street, with pines growing out of the paving and Tahtalı's cone rising straight behind. You can swim off the ancient quays where Alexander's fleet anchored, then dry off in a theatre that looks down onto the middle bay.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — swimmable water with a fraction of the August crowd
tip: Arrive at opening, park at the far south harbour rather than the entrance lot, and swim before the Kemer boats unload around 11:00.
todo: Swim from the south harbour quay
rev: The combination of ruins and swimming is what everyone raves about; the complaints are the ticket price for a small site, thin facilities and boat parties that take over the beaches at midday.
entry: €10 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 50 min on the D400 past Kemer; the site entrance is 2 km off the highway at Tekirova.

name: Tahtalı Dağı and the Olympos Cable Car
desc: A 2,365-metre limestone cone that stands almost directly over the sea, with a cable car climbing to the summit in ten minutes from Tekirova. From the top you see the whole Gulf of Antalya, the Beydağları ridgeline and, on clear winter days, snow on the terrace while people swim below.
season: All year — clearest Nov–Apr; summer afternoons haze over completely
tip: Take the earliest car of the day: cloud usually forms on the summit by late morning in summer and the view is gone.
todo: Sunset descent slot on the cable car
Watch paragliders launch from the top
rev: The ride and the view get consistent praise, but the ticket is expensive by Turkish standards, the summit is bitterly windy, and the whole trip is wasted if cloud sets in — check the webcam first.
entry: Around €40 return for foreigners; paragliding tandem from about €120
onward: Antalya (AYT) 45 min on the D400 to the Tekirova base station; shuttles run from Kemer and most Antalya hotels.

name: Beydağları Coastal National Park
desc: The park that ties this coast together: 700 square kilometres running from Kemer to Adrasan, taking in Phaselis, Olympos, the Chimaera and the whole seaward wall of the Bey mountains. Red pine and cedar to 2,000 metres, wild goats on the ridges, and canyons like Göynük cutting back from the sea.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — fire risk closes forest tracks in high summer
tip: Göynük canyon is the easy way in — the lower gorge is a two-hour wade and gets you the scenery without a full mountain day.
rev: Walkers rate the variety from beach to 2,000 metres in an hour; the recurring problems are unsigned forest junctions, summer fire closures and canyon operators overselling the Göynük trip.
entry: Free to enter; Göynük canyon around ₺350 (≈€8)
onward: Antalya (AYT), then the D400 south — Kemer, Çamyuva and Tekirova are all gateways; a car is essential for the mountain roads.

name: Lycian Way — Eastern Half
desc: From Finike to the outskirts of Antalya the trail leaves the beach resorts and climbs: Arycanda's terraces, the empty coast to Cape Gelidonya, the Chimaera flames, then the long haul over the shoulder of Tahtalı. Red-and-white flashes on rocks, village pensions, and stretches where you meet nobody for a day.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer on this section is dangerous, winter snow blocks the high traverses
tip: Carry four litres and plan around water: the cisterns marked on older maps between Karaöz and Adrasan are often dry by May.
todo: Adrasan over Musa Dağı to Olympos
Çıralı up to Ulupınar and the flames
rev: Walkers rate the eastern half as wilder and emptier than the west; complaints are patchy waymarking after forest fires, bulldozed sections replaced by road, and pensions that shut out of season.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT), then buses down the D400 drop you at Finike, Kumluca, Adrasan junction or Çıralı; taxis cover the last few kilometres.

name: Kaleiçi (Antalya Old Town)
desc: The walled old town falls in tight lanes of Ottoman wooden houses down to a Roman harbour still used by tour boats. Hadrian's Gate opens it at the top, the fluted Yivli minaret marks the skyline, and the Hıdırlık tower at the cliff edge is where the city goes to watch the sun set behind the Beydağları.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — July and August in the lanes are airless
tip: Walk in through Hadrian's Gate but leave by the Karaalioğlu park side, and eat one street back from the marina where prices halve.
todo: Kesik Minare and the Yivli minaret
Boat out of the Roman harbour
rev: The setting and the restored houses charm nearly everyone; the constant complaints are restaurant touts, marina prices, late-night bar noise for anyone sleeping there, and cobbles hostile to wheeled bags.
entry: Free to wander; individual museums ₺100–300 (≈€2–7)
onward: Antalya (AYT) is 15 km out — the tram from the airport line or a 20-minute taxi drops you at Hadrian's Gate; no cars inside the walls.

name: Düden Waterfalls
desc: Two entirely different falls on the same river. Upper Düden drops into a mossy basin with a walkway that takes you behind the curtain into a cave; Lower Düden throws itself forty metres off the travertine cliff straight into the sea at Lara, best seen from a boat or the clifftop park.
season: Mar–Jun after the snowmelt — flow drops sharply by late August
tip: Do the upper falls early on a weekday: at weekends the picnic park is full of Antalya families and the cave path becomes a queue.
todo: Clifftop view of the lower falls
Boat trip to see it from the sea
rev: An easy, genuinely impressive half-day; the gripes are two separate tickets and car parks, weekend crowds, and how thin the water runs at the end of a dry summer.
onward: Antalya (AYT) 20 min by taxi; city bus KL08 reaches the upper falls, and the lower falls are on the Lara road east of the centre.

name: Kurşunlu Waterfall
desc: An eighteen-metre fall dropping into a green pool at the head of a small wooded canyon, with seven smaller pools stepping down through pine and laurel below it. It is a nature park rather than a spectacle — terrapins on the rocks, squirrels in the pines, and shade the whole way round the loop.
season: Mar–Jun — the flow is weak by September and the pool goes murky
tip: Take the lower boardwalk loop past the small pools; most visitors photograph the main fall from the viewing terrace and drive away in fifteen minutes.
rev: A calm, shaded break from the coast heat; visitors warn that the fall is modest, that it can be reduced to a trickle in late summer, and that weekends bring coach parties.
entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a small vehicle fee
onward: Antalya (AYT) 15 min — it is 7 km inland from the airport off the Aksu road, easiest with a car or on a Perge–Aspendos tour.

name: Antalya Archaeological Museum
desc: Türkiye's best provincial collection: the Roman emperors and dancing girls hauled out of Perge's theatre, the Weary Herakles whose upper half came back from Boston in 2011, and a hall of sarcophagi carved with the labours of Hercules. It gives every Pamphylian ruin you visit its missing statuary.
season: All year — the obvious rainy-day plan on this coast
tip: Check before you go: the museum is closed for a full rebuild, and only a small selection is on temporary display elsewhere in the city.
rev: Rated by many as second only to Istanbul's; the dominant issue in 2026 is the long closure for reconstruction, and past visitors also complained about weak lighting and thin English labelling.
entry: €15 for foreigners when open · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye — closed for reconstruction, verify before travelling
onward: Antalya (AYT), then the T1 tram to Müze stop at the western end of Konyaaltı; a 10-minute walk from the cliff park.

name: Konyaaltı Beach
desc: Seven kilometres of grey pebble running west from the Antalya cliffs with the Beydağları rising straight out of the sea at the far end — the best mountain backdrop of any city beach in Türkiye. The water shelves fast and stays clear, and the promenade behind is all cafés and cycle path.
season: Jun–Oct for swimming; the promenade is pleasant all year
tip: Walk west past the Beach Park section: the free stretches nearer the Sarısu end are cleaner and a third of the price for sunbeds.
rev: Locals love the mountain view and the clean water; visitors complain that the pebbles hurt bare feet, that the drop-off is steep for children, and that the beach clubs charge city prices.
entry: Free on the public stretches; sunbed pairs from ₺400 (≈€9)
onward: Antalya (AYT), then the T1 tram or a 25-minute taxi to the western end; the whole beach is walkable from Kaleiçi in 20 minutes.

name: Lara Beach
desc: The sand side of Antalya: a long golden strip east of the city where the big themed resorts line up behind a public beach park. Shallow, warm and family-friendly, with the lower Düden falls tipping off the cliff at its western end and sand-sculpture festivals on the beach each summer.
season: Jun–Oct — August is hot, packed and expensive
tip: Use the municipal Lara Beach Park entrance rather than a hotel gate; it has proper showers, shade and a fraction of the cost.
todo: Lower Düden falls from the cliff path
Fish lunch at the beach park
rev: Praised for actual sand and calm water; the standard complaints are hotel-monopolised frontage, traffic on the Lara road, seaweed after storms and paying for everything twice in resort areas.
entry: Public beach park around ₺150 (≈€3.50) with a sunbed
onward: Antalya (AYT) is only 15 minutes away by taxi; city buses run the Lara road from the centre in about 30 minutes.

name: Karain Cave
desc: A vast dry cave mouth in a cliff above the Döşemealtı plain, occupied on and off for around 500,000 years — the longest human sequence in Anatolia. Three chambers, a small site museum with flint tools and Neanderthal teeth, and a terrace looking out over the plain that alone justifies the drive.
season: All year — a cool refuge in summer, though the track is slippery after rain
tip: Ask the guardian to unlock the third chamber; without asking you are shown only the first two and out in ten minutes.
todo: Climb the stone path to the mouth
Flint tools in the site museum
rev: Prehistory enthusiasts find it moving and almost empty; others complain the display is dated, the climb is steeper than expected and the finds themselves are mostly in Antalya.
entry: €5 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 40 min — take the Burdur road to Döşemealtı, then the signed lane through Yağca village; no public transport.

name: Perge
desc: The most legible Roman city on this coast: a stadium for twelve thousand, twin Hellenistic gate towers, and a colonnaded street running 300 metres with a water channel still cut down its middle and chariot ruts in the paving. The baths keep their marble floors and the whole grid is easy to read.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain hits 40 °C with zero shade in summer
tip: Start at the far end by the nymphaeum and walk downhill with the water channel; everyone else walks up into the sun and gives up halfway.
todo: Hellenistic gate and its oval court
rev: Consistently called better value than Ephesus for the space and quiet; the complaints are the total lack of shade, a closed theatre across the road and coach groups arriving mid-morning.
entry: €11 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Antalya (AYT) 15 min — it sits 2 km north of Aksu off the D400; the Antalya–Aksu dolmuş drops you at the junction.

name: Aspendos
desc: The best-preserved Roman theatre anywhere, built around 160 AD and still roofed by its own stage wall, seating seven thousand under an intact vaulted gallery. Behind it, most visitors miss the acropolis and one of the finest surviving Roman aqueducts, with two pressure towers standing in open fields.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the opera and ballet festival runs in September
tip: Walk the fifteen minutes uphill to the aqueduct and basilica behind the theatre — nine out of ten visitors never leave the auditorium.
todo: Clap once from the orchestra floor
Upper gallery for the full sweep
rev: The acoustics and preservation astonish people; the criticisms are heavy-handed restoration in concrete, souvenir stalls at the gate, and a bare hot site once you step outside the theatre.
entry: €15 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 45 min east on the D400, then 4 km inland at Serik; every Antalya–Side bus passes the junction.

name: Side
desc: A resort village built inside an ancient city, so a colonnaded street of souvenir shops runs past a 15,000-seat theatre and ends at the Temple of Apollo, whose five re-erected columns stand on the point with the sea behind them. The museum occupies the Roman baths by the agora.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the peninsula is shoulder-to-shoulder in August
tip: Photograph the Apollo columns twenty minutes before sunset from the western beach side, then eat away from the harbour where the menus are half the price.
todo: Side Museum in the Roman baths
rev: The mix of ruins, beach and restaurants sells itself; the complaints are relentless souvenir touting, tourist-menu food, traffic on the peninsula and rubbish around the fringes of the site.
entry: €10 for foreigners covering the ancient city and museum · Museum Pass Türkiye accepted
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 east on the D400 to Manavgat, then 4 km to the peninsula; buses run every 20 min from Manavgat otogar.

name: Termessos
desc: A Pisidian eyrie at 1,050 metres that Alexander looked at and decided not to besiege. The theatre hangs on the edge of a gorge with Güllük Dağı opposite, and the necropolis above is a chaos of sarcophagi thrown around by earthquakes, half-swallowed by pines and wild cyclamen.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — cool at altitude even when Antalya is at 40 °C
tip: Allow three hours and take water; the climb from the car park to the theatre is a solid thirty minutes up a rough stone path with no facilities on top.
todo: King's Road and the city walls
rev: Hikers call it the most dramatic ruin in Türkiye; the caveats are constant — a hard climb, no shade or café, vague signage, and mountain goats and snakes among the tombs.
entry: ₺350 (≈€8) including the national park · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 50 min on the Korkuteli road, then 9 km up a park road; no public transport, so drive or join a tour.

name: Selge
desc: A Pisidian city at 1,000 metres above the Köprülü canyon, where the village of Altınkaya has grown into the ruins — goats on the theatre steps, a farmhouse leaning on a temple wall. The approach through eroded limestone pinnacles is as memorable as the site, and a Roman bridge crosses the gorge below.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the last road is icy and sometimes closed in winter
tip: Village children will offer to guide you and sell you flowers; agree a price first, and take the drive slowly — the final 12 km is single-track with drops.
todo: Roman Oluk bridge over the gorge
Rock pinnacles on the approach road
rev: The setting and the near-total absence of other tourists are what people remember; the complaints are the nerve-testing road, persistent child sellers and almost no interpretation on site.
entry: Free — a small parking donation is usually asked
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h — the Beşkonak road up the Köprüçay, then the narrow climb past Oluk bridge; a car with decent clearance helps.

name: Köprülü Canyon
desc: Fourteen kilometres of gorge cut by the Köprüçay through cypress forest, with water cold enough to take your breath in August. It is Türkiye's rafting centre — grade II–III, wet and cheerful rather than frightening — and a Roman bridge still spans the narrowest point at Oluk.
season: Apr–Oct for rafting; May–Jun has the strongest flow after snowmelt
tip: Book the early morning run: by noon the river is a convoy of rafts and the riverside restaurants have queues an hour long.
todo: Trout lunch on a river platform
rev: A genuinely fun day and cheap by European standards; complaints are conveyor-belt operators, hard-sell photo packages, hour-long transfers and a river far busier than the brochures suggest.
entry: National park ₺100 (≈€2.30) per car; rafting packages €25–40 with transfer
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 30 via Serik and Beşkonak; almost everyone comes on an operator minibus from Side, Belek or Antalya.

name: Sillyon
desc: A flat-topped mesa rising out of the Pamphylian plain, fortified since Hellenistic times and never properly excavated. A landslide in 1969 took half the theatre down the slope, but the ramp gate, a Seljuk mosque and a stadium survive up top, along with the longest inscription in the Pamphylian dialect.
season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade, no water, and the plain bakes in summer
tip: Drive up to the village on the north side rather than attempting the old ramp from the south, and keep clear of the sheepdogs guarding the flocks on the plateau.
rev: For ruin-hunters it is the best empty site near Antalya; everyone warns about the unmarked approach, aggressive dogs, unstable cliff edges and the fact that nothing is signed or fenced.
entry: Free — unstaffed
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 40 min east, then 8 km of farm road north from the D400 near Serik; a car is essential.

name: Seleukeia (Pamphylia)
desc: A small Roman town lost in dense pine forest on a hill fifteen kilometres above Side, with an agora, baths and a market building whose relief frieze is still in place. Nobody sells tickets, birds are the only noise, and pine needles cover half the paving — the antidote to Side in August.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — pleasant in the forest shade even at midday
tip: Park at Bucakşeyhler village and take the marked path up; navigation apps often send cars onto a forest track that ends nowhere.
todo: Relief frieze on the market hall
rev: Those who find it call it a magical hour alone in the woods; the complaints are that it is genuinely hard to find, overgrown, and that the best reliefs are hidden behind scrub.
entry: Free — unstaffed
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 20 to Manavgat, then 15 km north through Bucakşeyhler; there is no bus and no signage from the main road.

name: Manavgat Waterfall
desc: Not high — barely four metres — but wide, and the whole Manavgat river pours over a limestone shelf in a solid white sheet under plane trees. The appeal is the terrace of tea gardens along the bank and the river boats that run down from the town bridge to the sea.
season: Apr–Jun for volume; the river runs lower and warmer by September
tip: Skip the ticketed viewing park and take the river boat from Manavgat bridge instead — you see the same water, plus the delta and the fish restaurants.
todo: Boat down to the river mouth
rev: Pleasant for an hour with cheap tea; almost every review notes that the fall is far smaller than expected, that the site is packed with coaches and stalls, and that it is not worth a long detour.
entry: ₺100 (≈€2.30) for the falls park
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 east on the D400; the falls are 3 km north of Manavgat, and dolmuşes run there from the otogar.

name: Titreyengöl
desc: A small lagoon a few hundred metres behind the Sorgun beach, ringed by umbrella pines — the name means the trembling lake, from the marshy ground that shivers underfoot. Storks and terrapins in the reeds at dawn, a walking loop under the trees, and a long sand beach on the far side of the pines.
season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the resort strip is saturated in August
tip: Walk the lake loop at first light before the hotel joggers and the pedalos; the far bank is where the herons stand.
todo: Pine forest path to Sorgun beach
Sunset drink on the lake terrace
rev: Guests of the surrounding all-inclusives rate the quiet and the pine shade; independent visitors complain the lakeshore is effectively hotel property and the water itself is stagnant and green in late summer.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 10 east on the D400, then 5 km south at Manavgat toward Sorgun; hotel shuttles serve the whole strip.

name: Altınbeşik Cave
desc: Türkiye's largest underground lake, entered by rowing boat from a cliff mouth high above the Manavgat gorge. Two hundred metres of flooded passage, travertine dams glowing under the lamps, and a hall where the guide kills the light and the water goes completely black and silent.
season: Mar–Jun when meltwater fills the lake; boats often stop running by late summer
tip: Ring the national park office at Ürünlü before driving up — when the water level is wrong the boats do not run and the trip is wasted.
rev: Those who catch it right describe it as unforgettable; the recurring complaints are wasted journeys when the boats are not operating, a rough final track and a very short visit for the drive involved.
entry: ₺200 (≈€4.50) including the boat
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h 30 via Manavgat and İbradı, then a steep 7 km down to Ürünlü; a car is essential.

name: Ormana
desc: A cedar-and-juniper village at 1,000 metres built in düğmeli or buttoned style — horizontal timbers slotted into stone without a nail, so the walls read like woven fabric. Perhaps sixty of the old houses survive, some restored as guesthouses, above a valley of walnut and mulberry trees.
season: May–Oct — snow closes some of the approach roads in midwinter
tip: Ask at the Ormana Antique House to see inside a restored buttoned house; from the street you only see the outer skin of the technique.
rev: Visitors are charmed by the architecture and the silence; the complaints are that a Turkish TV series brought weekend coach crowds, that several houses are derelict, and that food options are minimal.
entry: Free — the Antique House charges a small fee
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h 15 via Manavgat and the İbradı road; hire a car, since buses reach İbradı at best once a day.

name: İbradı
desc: Antalya's smallest district, a stone town of under three thousand people wedged into cedar forest at the top of the Manavgat gorge. The road up from the coast is the real attraction: an hour of switchbacks through the canyon with the river far below, ending in cold mountain air and walnut orchards.
season: May–Oct — winter brings snow and the gorge road ices over
tip: Drive up from Manavgat and come down via Akseki rather than doubling back; the loop takes in the gorge, Ormana and the cedar ridges in one day.
todo: Manavgat gorge road from the coast
Old stone houses in the centre
Trout lunch in a mountain village
rev: Travellers praise the drive and the temperature drop; the honest downsides are almost nothing to do in the town itself, very few beds and shops that shut at dusk.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT), then the D400 to Manavgat and 75 km north up the gorge road — about 2 h 15 in total by car.

name: Akseki
desc: A Taurus town at 1,000 metres whose surrounding villages — Sarıhacılar, Güçlüköy, Belenalan — keep some of the finest vernacular stone-and-timber architecture in Türkiye, all cantilevered upper floors and flat earth roofs. The Seljuk Ulu Camii sits in the centre and cedar ridges rise on every side.
season: May–Oct — heavy snow between December and March, though the town stays reachable
tip: The town is the base, not the sight: drive out to Sarıhacılar and Güçlüköy, where whole streets of old houses survive unrestored.
todo: Cedar forest walk above the town
rev: Rated highly by anyone interested in vernacular architecture and empty mountain roads; complaints are the long drive from the coast, depopulated villages and very limited accommodation.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h via Manavgat or 2 h 30 on the inland Konya road; buses run once or twice daily from Manavgat.

name: Çığlıkara Cedar Forest
desc: The largest Lebanon cedar forest left anywhere, spread over 15,000 hectares of karst above Elmalı at 1,400 to 1,900 metres. Some trees are more than a thousand years old, with flat plated crowns and trunks you cannot reach around; between them are sinkholes, wild peonies in May and complete silence.
season: May–Jun for wildflowers, Oct for colour — forest roads are snowbound Dec–Mar
tip: Head for the Dikmen and Sülekler sections off the Elmalı–Gömbe road; the marked thousand-year-old cedar is a short walk from a signed lay-by.
rev: Walkers describe it as the quietest forest in the country; the caveats are unsigned gravel roads, no facilities of any kind and closures when fire risk peaks in August.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h via Korkuteli to Elmalı, then the Gömbe road climbs straight into the reserve; a car is essential.

name: Saklıkent Ski Centre
desc: A modest ski area on Bakırlı Dağı at 1,850 to 2,400 metres, fifty kilometres from Antalya, whose selling point is entirely geographic: you can ski a north-facing run in the morning and swim at Konyaaltı in the afternoon. Three lifts, a handful of pistes, and the national observatory on the ridge above.
season: Jan–Mar for reliable snow; the road is fine but the season is short and unpredictable
tip: Go on a weekday — Antalya families fill the two chairlifts at weekends and the queue is longer than the run.
todo: Morning ski then afternoon sea swim
Snow view down to the Gulf of Antalya
rev: Novelty value is high and the day is cheap; skiers are blunt that the pistes are short, the snow is thin in warm winters and the equipment hire is basic.
entry: Day lift pass around ₺600 (≈€13) with hire extra
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 on the Korkuteli road, then the signed climb up Bakırlı; minibuses run from Antalya at weekends in season.

name: Elmalı
desc: An apple-growing town on a 1,100-metre plateau behind the Lycian mountains, with a bazaar of low wooden shopfronts and the elegant Ömerpaşa Mosque of 1610 tiled in İznik blue. The surrounding tumuli produced the painted Karaburun tomb and the disputed Elmalı hoard of Lycian coins.
season: May–Oct — hard frosts and snow from December, and the apple harvest is in September
tip: Time it for the Thursday market, when growers come down from the plateau villages and the square fills with apples, cheese and wooden tools.
todo: Old wooden houses off the bazaar
rev: Travellers heading to Gömbe or the cedars find it a genuine working town rather than a sight; complaints are limited food and lodging, and a centre that has lost many old buildings to concrete.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 45 via Korkuteli, or an hour up from Finike on the D635; regular buses run from Antalya otogar.

name: Avlan Lake
desc: A shallow plateau lake ringed by cedar-covered hills south of Elmalı, drained for farmland in the 1970s and deliberately refilled decades later after the microclimate collapsed. It now draws coot, grebes and migrating cranes, with picnic tables under the pines and mirror-flat water at dawn.
season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — levels drop in late summer and the shore turns to mud
tip: Stop on the Elmalı–Gömbe road at the northern picnic area rather than the main viewpoint; the birds are on that shallow end.
todo: Dawn reflections from the north shore
rev: A calm, free stop on the way to Gömbe that locals rate highly; visitors note the water level is unreliable, litter accumulates at the picnic areas and there is no infrastructure whatsoever.
entry: Free
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h via Korkuteli and Elmalı; the lake is 12 km south of Elmalı on the Kaş road, best reached by car.

name: Gömbe and Yeşil Göl
desc: A highland town at 1,050 metres under Akdağ, where Antalya escapes the August heat: plane-shaded tea gardens, trout ponds and cherry orchards. Above it a rough track climbs to Yeşil Göl, a green glacial tarn at 2,300 metres, and the Uçarsu waterfall drops off the rock wall nearby.
season: Jun–Sep for the high lake — snow blocks the upper track from November to May
tip: The last stretch to Yeşil Göl needs a high-clearance vehicle or a two-hour walk; village drivers in Gömbe run jeeps up for a fixed price.
todo: Jeep or walk up to Yeşil Göl
Uçarsu waterfall on the Akdağ wall
Trout under the plane trees in Gömbe
rev: People rate the cool air and the tarn walk highly; the complaints are the punishing track, weekend picnic litter at the lake and locals grazing right up to the shore.
entry: Free; jeep transfer to the lake around ₺1,200 (≈€27) per vehicle
onward: Antalya (AYT) about 3 h via Elmalı, or 1 h 30 up from Kaş on the D350; a car or a village jeep is the only way to the lake.

name: Alanya Castle
desc: Six kilometres of Seljuk wall wrapping a rock peninsula 250 metres above the sea, built by Alaeddin Keykubad after 1220. Inside are cisterns, a Byzantine chapel and a village of gardens; below stand the octagonal Red Tower and the five-bay dockyard, the only intact Seljuk shipyard left.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the climb in July heat is punishing
tip: Take the cable car up from Iskele and walk down through the Ehmedek quarter; the road up by taxi misses the whole inhabited part of the castle.
rev: The views and the scale impress; complaints are that the inner castle is largely ruins and gardens, the walk is long and shadeless, and the site has separate tickets for tower, shipyard and citadel.
entry: €12 for foreigners for the citadel · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye; cable car around ₺250 (≈€6)
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h on the D400; in town the cable car station is on the Iskele waterfront.

name: Damlataş Cave
desc: A small stalactite cave found by quarrymen in 1948 under the western cliff of the Alanya peninsula, with a chamber of orange-tinged columns fifteen metres down. Its constant 22 °C, 95 per cent humidity and high carbon dioxide are prescribed for asthma, and patients still sit inside for hours each morning.
season: All year — the cool interior is a relief in July and August
tip: It opens early for asthma treatment before general visiting, so arrive at opening if you want the chamber without a queue behind you.
rev: Cheap, cool and ten minutes long — which is exactly the complaint: many find it too small and too crowded for the queue, and the air is genuinely heavy for anyone claustrophobic.
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h; the cave is at the foot of the castle rock beside Cleopatra Beach, walkable from central Alanya.

name: Dim Çayı
desc: A cold mountain river fifteen kilometres east of Alanya, where restaurants build wooden platforms straight over the water and you eat trout with your feet in the current. Upstream the valley narrows below the Dim dam, and Dim Cave sits on the slope above with a 400-metre lit gallery.
season: Jun–Sep — the whole point is the cold water when the coast is at 38 °C
tip: Drive past the first cluster of platforms near the mouth: the places 8 km upstream are cheaper, quieter and the water there is properly cold.
todo: Lunch on a platform over the river
Swim in the pool below the dam
rev: A local favourite for escaping the heat; complaints are traffic and parking chaos at weekends, water cold enough to hurt, and platform restaurants that charge per person for the seat.
entry: Free along the river; Dim Cave ₺200 (≈€4.50)
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 30 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Alanya, then 15 km inland up the Kestel valley road; dolmuşes run in summer.

name: Sapadere Canyon
desc: A 750-metre boardwalk pinned to the wall of a narrow Taurus gorge above Alanya, ending at a waterfall and a pool that stays around 12 °C in August. Walls rise 400 metres on both sides, the light comes in slabs, and the drive up passes through goat villages and old terraced fields.
season: May–Oct — the walkway closes in winter and after heavy rain
tip: Get there before eleven; from midday the boardwalk becomes single-file with coach groups and the pool is unswimmable for the crowd.
todo: Walk the full boardwalk to the falls
Swim in the cold plunge pool
Trout lunch at the canyon mouth
rev: The gorge and the cold water get good reviews; the complaints are a long winding minibus transfer, an entrance fee for a short walk, and rails and concrete that make it feel managed.
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 45 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Alanya, then 40 km of mountain road inland; most people come on a half-day tour.

name: Cleopatra Beach
desc: Two kilometres of coarse pale sand on the western side of the Alanya peninsula, with the castle rock closing the view at one end. The grain is unusually large and light, the water deepens gently, and the legend that Mark Antony gave the beach to Cleopatra is repeated on every sign.
season: May–Oct — the water stays swimmable into November
tip: The far western end past the Atatürk statue is the least developed stretch, with the same sand and a fraction of the sunbeds.
todo: Sunset with the castle rock behind
Walk up to Damlataş cave from the sand
rev: Consistently rated the best city beach on this coast for water quality and Blue Flag standards; the complaints are density of sunbeds, loud beach bars and a promenade of identical tourist restaurants.
entry: Free; sunbed and umbrella around ₺400 (≈€9)
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h on the D400; the beach starts a five-minute walk west of central Alanya.

name: Gazipaşa
desc: The last town before the Mersin border, where the Taurus comes down to the sea and the coast turns wild. Banana and avocado terraces, empty shingle beaches at Koru and Kahyalar, the ruins of Selinus where the emperor Trajan died in 117, and none of the resort density of Alanya an hour west.
season: May–Oct for swimming; Mar–Apr for the coast road and the hills in flower
tip: Drive the D400 east from town toward Anamur for half an hour — the cliff corniche past Kaledran is the best coastal driving in the province.
todo: Selinus ruins and the Trajan cenotaph
Banana stalls on the coast road
rev: Travellers value the quiet and the prices next to Alanya; the honest downsides are little nightlife, patchy restaurant choice out of season and beaches with a strong undertow after wind.
entry: Free — Selinus is unstaffed
onward: Gazipaşa–Alanya (GZP) airport is 6 km from the town centre, with Alanya 45 min west on the D400.

name: Alara Castle and Alarahan
desc: A Seljuk caravanserai of 1232 sits by the Alara river with its courtyard and stables intact, while the castle above is reached by a rock-cut tunnel of some 120 dark steps spiralling inside the crag. At the top: cisterns, a bath and a view down the whole valley to the sea.
season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the tunnel climb is brutal in midsummer heat
tip: Bring a torch — the tunnel staircase to the castle is genuinely unlit, wet in places and the reason most visitors turn back.
todo: River platform lunch below the crag
rev: Those who make the climb rate it one of the best small sites in the region; complaints are the pitch-dark slippery tunnel, no railings, and a han partly given over to souvenir stalls.
entry: Free for the han; small fee for the castle path
onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 1 h or Antalya (AYT) 1 h 30 on the D400, then 9 km inland at the Alara river bridge west of Alanya.
